y-m-03-01.topic: Sorting standards: deciding on words that give the same result for everyone
y-m-03-01.goal: Understand that sorting with a word like 'big', whose boundary is not clear, can give different results for different people, and make and say a standard that gives the same result no matter who sorts.
y-m-03-01.material:
8 buttons are lined up in one row from the smallest to the biggest. From the left they are named 가, 나, 다, 라, 마, 바, 사, and 아. The buttons are all the same color and shape and differ only in size.
Mina gathered 라, 마, 바, 사, and 아 (5 buttons) as the 'big buttons'. Hajun gathered 마, 바, 사, and 아 (4 buttons) as the 'big buttons'. The two looked at the same row of buttons, and both sorted by the word 'big button'.
y-m-03-01.thinking.0: Think about why the results are different
y-m-03-01.thinking.1: Judge what else is needed to get the same result
y-m-03-01.thinking.2: Make a clear sorting standard yourself
y-m-03-01.prereq.0: Sorting objects by a set standard
y-m-03-01.s.s1.prompt: What is the most suitable reason why the big buttons gathered by the two people are different?
y-m-03-01.s.s1.hint.0: Write the big buttons the two people gathered side by side, and find which buttons are different.
y-m-03-01.s.s1.hint.1: Think about whether to put that button in the 'big buttons' or not, and if you were deciding, what you would look at to decide.
y-m-03-01.s.s1.explain: With only a word like 'big', where people can draw the line differently, it is hard to get the same result. Mina saw buttons from 라 on as 'big buttons', and Hajun saw buttons from 마 on as 'big'. Both sorted consistently by their own standard.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.prompt: For the two to get the same result from now on, what must be decided first?
y-m-03-01.s.s2.hint.0: Point again to where Mina and Hajun sorted differently.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.hint.1: Think about what the two people need to agree on so that they decide in exactly the same way which side to put it on at that spot.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.explain: Once it is decided from which button on counts as a 'big button', the dividing line is decided as one. There are many ways to decide it (for example, from button 라 on, or bigger than the middle button).
y-m-03-01.s.s3.prompt: Make and write a new way of saying how to sort the 'big buttons' so that the same result comes out no matter who sorts. Add a few words about why the same result comes out that way.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.hint.0: First decide which of the button names (가 to 아) to use as the boundary.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.hint.1: Read your words to a friend and imagine whether the same buttons come out.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.selfAssess.0: With the words you decided, is it decided as one which buttons are big buttons?
y-m-03-01.s.s3.selfAssess.1: If Mina and Hajun read my words, would they pick the same buttons?
y-m-03-01.s.s3.model.0: If you decide that buttons from 라 on are big buttons, the same result comes out no matter who sorts.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.model.1: If you say 'bigger than button 마', Mina and Hajun will sort in exactly the same way.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.model.2: Say a button is big if it is bigger than the middle button. Where to cut is decided, so everyone gets the same result.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.modelNote.2: If the row has two middle buttons, you need to decide one more time, such as 'the left one of the two middle buttons'.
y-m-03-01.title: The Same Row of Buttons, Different Groups of Big Buttons
y-m-03-01.s.s1.o.a: Mina has better eyesight than Hajun, so Mina's grouping is more accurate
y-m-03-01.s.s1.r.a: You saw it as a matter of good or poor eyesight. Both people looked at the same row and grouped using the word 'big', so the difference was where the line of the word lies.
y-m-03-01.s.s1.o.b: They counted the number wrong, so if they count again the two people's results will be the same
y-m-03-01.s.s1.r.b: You saw it as a counting mistake. The difference between 5 and 4 might be because of a counting mistake, but it might also be because they differed on where to start calling a button a 'big button'.
y-m-03-01.s.s1.o.c: Hajun didn't know the meaning of 'big', so only Hajun is wrong and Mina is right
y-m-03-01.s.s1.r.c: You saw it as only one person being wrong. Both people grouped consistently by their own criterion.
y-m-03-01.s.s1.o.d: It is not settled by the word alone which button 'big' starts from, so they drew the line differently
y-m-03-01.s.s1.r.d: You turned your attention to where the word 'big' splits. This is thinking that examined the boundary of the word that serves as the criterion.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.o.a: Have the two people decide by the same method which button to count as 'big button' from
y-m-03-01.s.s2.r.a: You turned your attention to where the dividing line is. You chose what is needed to make the criterion one.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.o.b: Instead of 'big button', call it by a stronger word such as 'very big button'
y-m-03-01.s.s2.r.b: People can also see differently where 'very big' starts. If you only change the word, the boundary is still not settled.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.o.c: Compare the results the two people grouped and follow the one with the larger count
y-m-03-01.s.s2.r.c: This row is settled to one result, but for other rows of buttons it can differ again. It does not settle the meaning of 'big'.
y-m-03-01.s.s2.o.d: One person groups first and the other groups following
y-m-03-01.s.s2.r.d: You thought about the order of grouping. If you group following, you are just copying one person's line, and the criterion is not settled.
y-m-03-01.s.s3.model.3: If you call a button at least twice as big as the smallest button a big button and group by measuring with a ruler, the same result comes out no matter who groups.

y-m-03-02.title: I split them into two boxes, but the cards increased
y-m-03-02.topic: Looking at overlaps and gaps in sorting results
y-m-03-02.goal: Understand that if the names of the sorted boxes overlap or some cards fit in no box, the counted result can differ from the total, and fix the sorting to one where every card goes in only one place.
y-m-03-02.material:
There are 9 cards in all. The card names and the numbers of cards are as follows.
[Cards] Red circle 3 cards / Blue circle 2 cards / Red triangle 2 cards / Blue triangle 2 cards (total 9 cards)
Seoa made two boxes. One is the 'red card box' and the other is the 'circle card box'. She looked at the cards one by one and put each card that fits a box into that box. Cards that fit neither box were left on the desk.
y-m-03-02.thinking.0: Finding a statement without a reason in the solution
y-m-03-02.thinking.1: Looking at whether the sorting names overlap
y-m-03-02.thinking.2: Comparing several ways to fix it
y-m-03-02.prereq.0: Sorting and counting objects by color or shape
y-m-03-02.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of numbers around 10
y-m-03-02.s.s1.prompt: This is Seoa's thinking. Pick the line that has a place that is hard to trust.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.hint.0: Pick up one red circle card and check one at a time which of the two boxes it can go in.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.hint.1: Separate the cards in the boxes from the cards left on the desk and write the number of cards for each.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.line.1: The red card box has 5 cards and the circle card box has 5 cards.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.line.2: 5 and 5 together make 10, so there are 10 cards in the boxes.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.line.3: There are 10 cards in the boxes, so there are 10 cards, not 9.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.line.4: I split them into two boxes with none left out, so the sorting was done well.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the ways to fix it so that every card goes in only one box.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write the two box names side by side and look for cards that fit both names.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.hint.1: For each fixed box, mark how many times each of the four kinds of cards goes in.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.o.d: Split into two boxes: red cards and blue cards
y-m-03-02.s.s2.r.d: You made two boxes with the other standard (color) and checked whether every card goes in only one place.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.explain: If you make boxes with one standard (only shape, or only color), every card goes in exactly one place. With the shape standard it is 5 circles and 4 triangles, and with the color standard it is 5 red and 4 blue. The sum is 9 cards in both.
y-m-03-02.s.s3.prompt: Woojin said, 'A red circle can go in both boxes, so we can use the first way as it is.' How would you answer Woojin? Use the red circle cards as an example and put in numbers.
y-m-03-02.s.s3.hint.0: Count and write how many times the 3 red circle cards go into which box.
y-m-03-02.s.s3.hint.1: Put the numbers of cards in the two boxes and the total number of cards side by side and compare them.
y-m-03-02.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Is it clear in the numbers you wrote that 5+5=10 is different from 9 cards?
y-m-03-02.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Does your reason why you must not use the first way as it is include words like 'counted twice'?
y-m-03-02.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Does it also include at least one way to fix it?
y-m-03-02.s.s3.model.0: The 3 red circles go in both the red box and the circle box, so they are counted twice. So it becomes 5+5=10, which is different from the 9 cards.
y-m-03-02.s.s3.model.1: You have to split by only one thing. The red circles go in both boxes, so they overlap. If you split only by shape, it is 5 circles and 4 triangles, so the sum is 9 cards.
y-m-03-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3: the 3 red circles fit both the 'red card box' and the 'circle card box', so they were counted twice. So 10, the sum of 5 and 5, is not the number of cards. Line 4: the increase of the 10 counted in the boxes is because of counting the same cards twice. It is not that the 9 cards counted at first were wrong. Line 5: the 2 blue triangles cannot go into any box, so they are left on the desk. So 'without leaving any out' is also not right. Lines 1 and 2 state the counted result as it is, so they are fine.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.o.a: Divide into two boxes, circle cards and triangle cards
y-m-03-02.s.s2.r.a: You made two boxes by one criterion (shape) and checked that every card goes in only one place.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.o.b: Divide into three boxes: red cards, circle cards, triangle cards
y-m-03-02.s.s2.r.b: You thought making more boxes would solve it. Even among the three boxes, a red circle fits two places, 'red' and 'circle'.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.o.c: Take away the 2 blue triangle cards without counting them
y-m-03-02.s.s2.r.c: You tried to make the sum match by removing the cards that don't fit. If you remove them, you haven't classified the cards but reduced them.
y-m-03-02.s.s2.o.e: Put the 3 overlapping cards only in the red card box
y-m-03-02.s.s2.r.e: If you put the overlapping cards on only one side, double counting is reduced. But the blue triangle cards still have nowhere to go.

y-m-03-03.title: Can one group's table tell about the whole class?
y-m-03-03.topic: The range that collected data can tell: one group and the whole class
y-m-03-03.goal: Understand that the survey results of only some friends cannot settle the whole class, say what else you need to know, and change your statement when more data is collected.
y-m-03-03.material:
Our class has 20 students, in 4 groups of 5. We decided that each person would pick one favorite snack and we would survey by group. Right now only Group 1's result is out.
[Group 1] Tteokbokki 3 students / Snacks 1 student / Fruit 1 student (total 5 students)
Doyun said, "The snack our class likes best is tteokbokki!"
y-m-03-03.thinking.0: Judge the range that the data tells
y-m-03-03.thinking.1: Judge whether the information is enough and say the information needed
y-m-03-03.thinking.2: Fix the first statement with new data
y-m-03-03.prereq.0: Counting data by kind and reading a table
y-m-03-03.prereq.1: Comparing sizes of numbers up to 20
y-m-03-03.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Doyun's words based on this table alone?
y-m-03-03.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many students' results the table has, and write that next to the number of students in the whole class.
y-m-03-03.s.s1.hint.1: Looking at the table, write in two lines what you can say for sure and what you do not know yet.
y-m-03-03.s.s1.o.c: It is only 5 students, so this table can tell nothing
y-m-03-03.s.s1.r.c: You thought the data is useless because it is small. You can know that within Group 1, tteokbokki is the most.
y-m-03-03.s.s1.o.d: The snack and fruit with 1 student each can be treated as none
y-m-03-03.s.s1.r.d: You treated the small boxes as none. Even 1 student is a person's choice and has to be counted.
y-m-03-03.s.s1.explain: What this table tells is the result of the 5 students in Group 1. We do not yet know the results of 15 of the 20 students in the whole class. You can say that within Group 1, tteokbokki is the most.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.prompt: To say which snack the whole class likes best, choose all the things you need to know more.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.hint.0: Write the difference between the number of people you know now and the number of people you want to know.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.hint.1: Think one by one about whether each choice changes the 'number for a snack' or not.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.explain: To talk about the whole class you need the results of the other 15 students, and you need to know whether each person picked only one thing to check that the counted numbers match 20 students.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.prompt:
The results of the other groups are out too.
[Group 2] Tteokbokki 1 student / Snacks 3 students / Fruit 1 student
[Group 3] Tteokbokki 1 student / Snacks 3 students / Fruit 1 student
[Group 4] Tteokbokki 2 students / Snacks 1 student / Fruit 2 students
Putting the four groups together, it is tteokbokki 7 students, snacks 8 students, and fruit 5 students (total 20 students). Write how it would be good to fix Doyun's first statement, using numbers.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write the snack that is the most in the Group 1 result and in the four-group result, and compare them.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.hint.1: Write how many students apart snacks and tteokbokki are, and think about how to say that difference.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Are the numbers 8 and 7 you wrote the same as the ones taken from the table?
y-m-03-03.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you write the difference between what you said from Group 1's result and what you said from the four groups' result?
y-m-03-03.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about how to say that 8 and 7 are 1 student apart?
y-m-03-03.s.s3.model.0: Doyun's words were wrong because they looked at only the 5 students in Group 1. When all 20 students are put together, it is tteokbokki 7 students and snacks 8 students, so snacks are the most.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.model.1: Snacks are 8 students and tteokbokki is 7 students, a difference of 1 student. Snacks are the most, but they are almost the same, so it is good to say that many also like tteokbokki.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.modelNote.1: Did not say only 'many' but added the point that the difference is 1 student.
y-m-03-03.s.s1.o.a: In Group 1, tteokbokki is the most, and we don't yet know about the whole class
y-m-03-03.s.s1.r.a: You separated what the table tells (Group 1) from what we don't yet know (the whole class).
y-m-03-03.s.s1.o.b: You can say that tteokbokki is the most in the whole class too
y-m-03-03.s.s1.r.b: You moved the result of 5 people straight over to the result of all 20. You have not yet seen the results of the other 15.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.o.a: How much one bowl of tteokbokki costs
y-m-03-03.s.s2.r.a: You turned your attention to the price. The price has nothing to do with which snack more people chose.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.o.b: The snacks chosen by the 15 people in the other 3 groups
y-m-03-03.s.s2.r.b: You examined that the results of the friends you have not yet seen are needed.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.o.c: Whether any friend in the other groups was left out of the survey
y-m-03-03.s.s2.r.c: You checked whether all 15 were included in the survey. If any friend is missing, it is hard to call it the result for the whole class.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.o.d: What the names of the friends in Group 1 are
y-m-03-03.s.s2.r.d: You turned your attention to the names. Names do not change which snack has how many people.
y-m-03-03.s.s2.acc.0: The results of the other 15 people are needed most. It would also be good to check, when gathering those results, that no friend is left out.
y-m-03-03.s.s3.model.2: The claim that tteokbokki is the most is wrong; if you gather the four groups, snacks have 8 people, 1 more than tteokbokki's 7.

y-m-03-04.title: How can I show it to a younger sibling who can't read numbers yet?
y-m-03-04.topic: Showing the same data with a table and a circle picture
y-m-03-04.goal: Understand that the same data can be shown with a table and with a circle picture, compare which suits which reader, and write words that explain it to a younger sibling.
y-m-03-04.material:
We surveyed the favorite seasons of 12 students in our class. Each person picked only one season.
[Table] Spring 4 students / Summer 5 students / Fall 1 student / Winter 2 students (total 12 students)
We also showed the same data as a circle picture. Under each season name, circles (○) are stacked upward as many as the number of friends who picked it. Spring has 4 circles stacked, summer has 5, fall has 1, and winter has 2.
y-m-03-04.thinking.0: Choosing a way of expressing that suits the receiver
y-m-03-04.thinking.1: Comparing the good points and inconvenient points of two ways of expressing
y-m-03-04.thinking.2: Turning what you can tell from the picture into words
y-m-03-04.prereq.1: Comparing sizes of numbers (10 or less)
y-m-03-04.s.s1.prompt: To tell a younger sibling who can't read numbers well yet which season is the most, what is best?
y-m-03-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write separately what the younger sibling 'can read' and what is 'hard to read'.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.hint.1: Compare what you need to look at in the table and in the picture to find the season with the most.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.o.a: Point to the season where the circles are stacked highest
y-m-03-04.s.s1.r.a: You thought that you can compare height with your eyes even without knowing numbers. You chose a method that suits the receiver.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.o.b: Show the numbers of the table written big
y-m-03-04.s.s1.r.b: You thought of writing the numbers big. If the younger sibling cannot read numbers yet, it is hard to read even if they are big.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.o.c: Show the table and read the numbers out loud
y-m-03-04.s.s1.r.c: You thought of reading it out loud. They can know by hearing, but it may be hard for the younger sibling to compare by themselves.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.o.d: Say only that there are 12 students in all
y-m-03-04.s.s1.r.d: You thought of saying only the total number. The total number does not tell the difference between seasons.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.explain: A circle picture can be compared by height even if you can't read numbers. Reading out the numbers from the table can also be a way to tell the younger sibling, but the picture is easier for the sibling to compare by themselves.
y-m-03-04.s.s1.acc.0: If you read the numbers out loud, the younger sibling can hear them even if they can't read numbers. But an adult would be doing the comparing for them. In this situation, the picture is easier if you want them to compare by themselves.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.prompt: Choose all the times when a circle picture is less convenient than a table.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what you have to do to find the exact number in a circle picture.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.hint.1: Imagine what the picture would be like if 100 friends picked.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.o.a: When there are few boxes because only four seasons were surveyed
y-m-03-04.s.s2.r.a: You thought of when there are few boxes. When there are few boxes, the picture is actually easier to see.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.o.b: When finding the season with the most at a glance and comparing
y-m-03-04.s.s2.r.b: You thought of comparing height with your eyes. A circle picture is good at this kind of job.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.r.c: You looked at the point that all the circles have to be drawn. When the number is very large, it is hard to draw and hard to count.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.o.d: When you have to write the exact number as a numeral
y-m-03-04.s.s2.r.d: You looked at recording the exact number. In a table, the number is written directly as a numeral.
y-m-03-04.s.s2.explain: A circle picture is good for comparing more and less at a glance, but when the number is very large it is hard to draw, and you have to count to know the exact number. A table can write the exact number directly.
y-m-03-04.s.s3.prompt: Write words that show the younger sibling the circle picture and tell them which season is the most. Also write how they can tell from the picture.
y-m-03-04.s.s3.hint.0: Compare by pointing with your finger at the rows of circles for different seasons.
y-m-03-04.s.s3.hint.1: First write words that answer the younger sibling's question, 'Where should I look?'
y-m-03-04.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Could a younger sibling who doesn't know numbers read (or hear) and understand the words you wrote?
y-m-03-04.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is it clear which part of the picture to look at?
y-m-03-04.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you explain the meaning of 'the most' with 'height' or 'number of circles'?
y-m-03-04.s.s3.model.0: See how summer is stacked the highest? Summer, with the most circles stacked, is the season the most friends picked.
y-m-03-04.s.s3.model.1: Look at summer. It has 5 circles, so its row is the longest. So the most friends picked summer.
y-m-03-04.s.s3.modelNote.1: The number 5 was said together, but the method of comparing by height is also there.

y-m-03-05.title: Making a box of number cards split between two pouches
y-m-03-05.topic: Sorting number cards by two conditions
y-m-03-05.goal: Sort number cards by the two conditions 'greater than' and 'less than', make several different boxes that fit the conditions, and say how you chose.
y-m-03-05.thinking.0: Think about the boundary of a condition (whether the same number is included)
y-m-03-05.thinking.1: Make several answers within the limits
y-m-03-05.thinking.2: Explain the way you chose using numbers
y-m-03-05.prereq.0: Comparing the sizes of numbers up to 20
y-m-03-05.prereq.1: The meaning of 'greater than' and 'less than'
y-m-03-05.s.s1.prompt: Can number card 15 be counted as a 'number less than 15' card?
y-m-03-05.s.s1.hint.0: Compare 15 and 14, 15 and 15, and 15 and 16, and say one by one whether each is 'less than 15'.
y-m-03-05.s.s1.hint.1: Underline that you compare with the number right before the word 'than'.
y-m-03-05.s.s1.o.a: Yes, 15 is 15 or less, so it is included in numbers less than 15
y-m-03-05.s.s1.r.a: You thought the same number is included in 'less'. 'Less than' does not include the same number.
y-m-03-05.s.s1.o.b: Yes, 15 is greater than 14, so it is included in the smaller numbers
y-m-03-05.s.s1.r.b: You compared with 14. To tell whether it is less 'than 15', you have to compare with 15.
y-m-03-05.s.s1.explain: 15 is the same as 15. 'Numbers less than 15' include only numbers less than 15, so 15 is not included. In the same way, 10 is not included in 'numbers greater than 10'.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.prompt: Choose 5 different cards from number cards 1 to 20 and make a box. In the box, there must be exactly 3 cards that are 'numbers greater than 10' and exactly 4 cards that are 'numbers less than 15'. Make 2 boxes with different cards.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on one number card and check whether it is counted in condition 1 and in condition 2.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.hint.1: First think about what number the remaining 1 card must be if there are 4 cards that are 'numbers less than 15'.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.ok.c1: All the cards are natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.fail.c1: The cards must be natural numbers from 1 to 20.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.fail.c2: There are two cards of the same number. There is only one of each card.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.ok.c3: There are exactly 3 cards that are 'numbers greater than 10'.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.fail.c3: There are not 3 cards that are 'numbers greater than 10'. 10 is not greater than 10.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.ok.c4: There are exactly 4 cards that are 'numbers less than 15'.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.fail.c4: There are not 4 cards that are 'numbers less than 15'. 15 is not less than 15.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.explain: For example, with 3, 7, 12, 13, and 16, the numbers greater than 10 are 12, 13, and 16, which is 3 cards, and the numbers less than 15 are 3, 7, 12, and 13, which is 4 cards. Also 1, 10, 11, 14, and 20 work. Two boxes become different boxes even if you change just one card.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.prompt: Explain how you chose the cards, using numbers.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.hint.0: Split the 5 cards in your box into three groups and write them: 'up to 10', '11 to 14', and 'from 15'.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.hint.1: Count how many cards are in each group and compare with the conditions.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Did you say how many cards of your 5 chosen cards satisfy condition 1 and condition 2 each?
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you say how you handled boundary numbers like 15 and 10?
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.model.0: I chose only one card that is not less than 15, the 16. There must be 4 cards less than 15, so I made the other 4 cards the numbers less than 15: 3, 7, 12, and 13.
y-m-03-05.s.s2.because.model.1: I chose 12, 13, and 16 so there are 3 numbers greater than 10, and chose 3 and 7 for the rest. The numbers less than 15 are 3, 7, 12, and 13, so that is 4 cards.
y-m-03-05.material:
There are number cards from 1 to 20, one of each (there is only one card of each number). Choose 5 cards and put them in one box. Suppose we count the cards in the box by two conditions.
Condition 1: Count how many cards are 'numbers greater than 10'.
Condition 2: Count how many cards are 'numbers less than 15'.
One card can be counted in both condition 1 and condition 2.
y-m-03-05.s.s1.o.c: 15 is not in this box, so we can't judge
y-m-03-05.s.s1.r.c: You turned your attention to whether the card is there. You can think ahead about what happens if 15 is put in the box, by comparing with 15.
y-m-03-05.s.s1.o.d: No, 15 is the same as 15, so it is not less than 15
y-m-03-05.s.s1.r.d: You judged 'less than' by comparing with 15. You examined the boundary that the same number is not included.

y-m-03-06.title: If the row is long, are there more cards?
y-m-03-06.topic: Comparing numbers: are the length of a row and the number the same?
y-m-03-06.goal: Understand that you cannot say there are more just because a row is long, and say ways to compare numbers by pairing one by one or counting, and when comparing by length is okay.
y-m-03-06.material:
Minseo put circle cards that are all the same size in two rows. In the top row she spread the cards far apart, and in the bottom row she put the cards touching each other. By eye, the top row is longer than the bottom row. She has not yet counted the cards.
Seohyeon said, "The top row is longer, so the top row has more cards!"
y-m-03-06.thinking.0: Think about whether the first judgment has a reason
y-m-03-06.thinking.1: Change your judgment with new information
y-m-03-06.thinking.2: Say it with a condition added
y-m-03-06.prereq.1: Comparing more and fewer by matching one to one
y-m-03-06.s.s1.prompt: What do you think of Seohyeon's words?
y-m-03-06.s.s1.hint.0: First look at whether the gaps between cards in the top row and the bottom row are the same or different.
y-m-03-06.s.s1.hint.1: Draw a case where the row length can be different even with the same number of cards.
y-m-03-06.s.s1.o.a: It's right. If a row is long, it has more cards
y-m-03-06.s.s1.r.a: You turned the length of the row into the number of cards. If you spread the cards far apart, the row can be long even with fewer cards.
y-m-03-06.s.s1.o.b: The bottom row is touching, so the bottom row has more cards
y-m-03-06.s.s1.r.b: You decided just by looking at the shape of being close together. You cannot say there are more cards just because they are touching.
y-m-03-06.s.s1.o.c: The number of cards in the two rows is the same
y-m-03-06.s.s1.r.c: You decided they are the same, but you have not counted yet. You need a reason for saying they are the same.
y-m-03-06.s.s1.o.d: You can't decide which row has more by length alone
y-m-03-06.s.s1.r.d: You thought of the length you see and the number of cards separately. You noticed that a method other than length is needed.
y-m-03-06.s.s1.explain: If the gaps between cards are wide, the row looks long even with fewer cards. The row length alone cannot decide which side has more cards. You have to count them or pair them up one by one.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.prompt: Seohyeon paired the cards of the top row and the bottom row one by one and joined them with lines. Every card in the top row got a partner, and 2 cards without a partner were left in the bottom row. Which row has more cards?
y-m-03-06.s.s2.hint.0: Mark separately the cards with a partner and the cards without a partner in the top row and the bottom row.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.hint.1: Say which row the cards without a partner are in.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.r.a: You carried on with the first impression that the row is long. Look again at which row has the cards left over when paired.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.r.b: You looked at the side with the leftover cards in the pairing. You judged more and fewer by the result of matching one to one.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.o.c: The two rows are the same
y-m-03-06.s.s2.r.c: You missed the information that cards without a partner were left over. If there are leftover cards, they are not the same number.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.r.d: You did not trust pairing as a way to compare. The side with the cards left without a partner has more.
y-m-03-06.s.s2.explain: When you pair one by one, the row with cards left without a partner has more cards. Pairing can be used whether the row is long or short.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.prompt: How would you like to tell Seohyeon? Write why you must not compare by the row's length, and the way to compare the number of cards.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.hint.0: Draw rows with the same number of cards for the case where the cards are spread far apart and the case where they are put touching.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.hint.1: Write in one sentence what you want to say while showing that picture to Seohyeon.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Does the reason you wrote mean 'the gaps between cards are different, so the length is different'?
y-m-03-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Is your way of comparing the number of cards concrete (counting, pairing)?
y-m-03-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about when comparing by length is okay (when all the gaps between cards are the same)?
y-m-03-06.s.s3.model.0: If you spread the cards far apart, the row gets long even with fewer cards. Count the cards one by one or pair them top and bottom.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.model.1: You can't know by length. It depends on whether they are touching or spread apart. Pair the cards of the top row and bottom row one by one, and the side with leftovers has more.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: It is fine to write only one way and not both.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.model.2: If the gaps between the cards are all the same, you can compare by length, but these rows have different gaps. So you have to count.
y-m-03-06.s.s3.modelNote.2: Added the condition under which comparing by length is okay.

y-m-03-07.title: What can we say while the results come in one by one?
y-m-03-07.topic: Fixing your judgment about 'the most' while the data is being collected
y-m-03-07.goal: Understand that it is hard to settle 'the most' before all the results are in, fix your judgment each time a new result comes out, and say the difference together when the results are close.
y-m-03-07.material: The 24 students in our class each picked one game they want to play at lunchtime. The games are three: jump rope, tag, and ball play. 4 groups (6 students in each group) report their results one group at a time. Before the results of all 24 students are in, we want to guess which game our class picked the most.
y-m-03-07.thinking.0: Fixing your judgment each time the data grows
y-m-03-07.thinking.1: Counting the part not yet known
y-m-03-07.thinking.2: Saying the size of the difference together
y-m-03-07.prereq.0: Counting data and reading a table
y-m-03-07.prereq.1: Comparing the sizes of numbers around 25
y-m-03-07.s.s1.prompt: The results are revealed one group at a time. Choose how you guess each time.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.hint.0: At each step, write the number of people who picked each game side by side and compare which game is ahead.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.hint.1: Count how many people whose results you do not yet know are left, and think about whether the order can change if those people all crowd onto one game.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.info:
This is the result of the 6 students in Group 1.
Jump rope 3 students / Tag 2 students / Ball play 1 student
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you guess the game picked the most among our 24 students?
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.after: The result of 6 students is only a part of the 24. Right now jump rope is ahead, but it can change when we see the results of the other 18.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You moved the result of 6 students straight over to the result of all 24. You have not yet seen the results of 18 students.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Right now jump rope is ahead, but we need to see the results of the other 18
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: You said separately what you know now and what you do not know yet.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: You thought the data is useless because it is small. It is a result that tells you jump rope is ahead among those 6.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: You decided they are the same without a reason. In Group 1, the number who picked was different for each game.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.info:
The result of the 6 students in Group 2 was added.
Group 2: Jump rope 0 students / Tag 4 students / Ball play 2 students
Putting together the 12 so far, it is jump rope 3 students / tag 6 students / ball play 3 students. The results of 12 more students are still left.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.after: So far, tag is ahead. But if the remaining 12 crowd onto one side, jump rope or ball play can pass tag, so it is too early to say it is decided yet.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.o.a: Tag has the most at 6 students, so it's decided to be tag
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: You saw the results so far as the final result. If all the remaining 12 pick jump rope, jump rope would be 15 and pass tag's 6.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: You are holding on to the first result as it is. If you add the newly collected results, tag is ahead now.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.o.c: Tag is ahead now, but we need to see the remaining 12
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: You fixed your first judgment to fit the new result, and also thought that 12 students are still unknown.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: You treated the game with 3 students as if it did not exist. If the remaining 12 pick, the order can change.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.info:
The results of the 12 students in Group 3 and Group 4 have come in too.
Group 3: Jump rope 3 students / Tag 2 students / Ball play 1 student
Group 4: Jump rope 2 students / Tag 1 student / Ball play 3 students
Putting all 24 together, it is jump rope 8 students / tag 9 students / ball play 7 students.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.ask: How would be good to say the result?
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.after: When all 24 are gathered, tag with 9 students is the most. It is only 1 student apart from jump rope's 8, so it is more accurate to also say that they are nearly the same.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: You read the game with the most correctly. But it is more accurate to also say the difference from jump rope.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.o.b: Tag is much more than the other games, so it is surely tag
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.r.b: You saw the difference between 9 and 8 as 'much'. You made a 1-student difference sound big.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.o.c: Jump rope was ahead in Group 1, so say it's jump rope
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: You are holding on to the first result. The result with all 24 put together has come out.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.o.d: Tag is the most, but it is only 1 student apart from jump rope
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: You said the game with the most and the size of the difference together. This idea also looked at the size of the result.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.reflect: How did 'the game with the most' change between looking at only the Group 1 result and when all 24 were gathered? How is it good to speak when the results are not all gathered?
y-m-03-07.s.s2.prompt: Write in one or two sentences words that announce the results of the 24 students to your classmates. Put in numbers, and also write the comparison between the game with the most and the other games.
y-m-03-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write the results of the 24 students for the three games side by side and find the difference between the most and the second most.
y-m-03-07.s.s2.hint.1: Read it to see whether a friend receiving the announcement could understand it from the numbers alone.
y-m-03-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Are the numbers you wrote the same as the result table (8 students, 9 students, 7 students)?
y-m-03-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you put into your words that the difference between the game with the most and jump rope is small?
y-m-03-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Did you think about what is different from the first guess?
y-m-03-07.s.s2.model.0: Tag is 9 students, jump rope is 8 students, and ball play is 7 students, so tag is the most. But it is only 1 student apart from jump rope, so they are nearly the same.
y-m-03-07.s.s2.model.1: When I gathered all 24 results, tag is the most with 9 students. Jump rope with 8 students is close, so I think it would be nice to play jump rope sometimes too.
y-m-03-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: Compared the difference and added a suggestion.
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Jump rope was decided to be the most common game, so there is no need to look further
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: The result of 6 people is small and of no use, so don't look at it
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The number of people who chose each of the three games will all be equally large
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.o.b: Jump rope was ahead at first, so jump rope will be the most to the end
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.1.o.d: Jump rope and ball play have only 3 people, so we can now leave them out and think
y-m-03-07.s.s1.st.2.o.a: If you add up all 24 people, tag is the most

y-m-03-08.title: I wish for a table like this: making a table that fits the conditions
y-m-03-08.topic: Making a survey table that fits conditions and what a table can tell
y-m-03-08.goal: Make several different tables that satisfy all the conditions of sum and order, and tell apart what you can say for sure from a table and what you cannot say.
y-m-03-08.material:
12 friends in a group each picked one place they want to go on a field trip. The places are three: the zoo, the amusement park, and the museum. Each person picked only one place. We do not know the result yet. But we set conditions for the kind of table we wish for.
Condition 1: At least 1 student picked each of the three places.
Condition 2: The sum of the three places is 12 students.
Condition 3: The zoo has more than the amusement park, and the amusement park has more than the museum.
Condition 4: The zoo and the amusement park do not differ by more than 2 students.
y-m-03-08.thinking.0: Making a table that satisfies several conditions at once
y-m-03-08.thinking.1: Checking that there are several solutions
y-m-03-08.thinking.2: Telling apart the range that a table tells
y-m-03-08.prereq.0: Adding numbers up to 20 and comparing sizes
y-m-03-08.prereq.1: Reading and talking about a table
y-m-03-08.s.s1.prompt: Make 2 different tables that fit the conditions. Write the number of friends who picked the zoo, the amusement park, and the museum.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.hint.0: Using the fact that the zoo is the most and the museum is the least, first decide one number for the amusement park.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.hint.1: Check whether the numbers you decided add up to 12, and if not, change the number for one place.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.ok.c1: All three places have at least 1 student.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.fail.c1: All three places must have at least 1 student (a natural number).
y-m-03-08.s.s1.ok.c2: The sum of the three places is 12 students.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.fail.c2: The sum of the three places is not 12 students.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.ok.c3: The order is the zoo the most and the museum the least.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.fail.c3: The zoo must be more than the amusement park, and the amusement park more than the museum.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.ok.c4: The difference between the zoo and the amusement park is 2 students or less.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.fail.c4: The zoo and the amusement park differ by more than 2 students.
y-m-03-08.s.s1.explain: There are three tables that fit the conditions: (6, 4, 2), (5, 4, 3), (6, 5, 1). The sum is 12 and the order is set, so there are not many possible numbers.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.prompt: Looking at the table you made (for example, zoo 6 students, amusement park 4 students, museum 2 students), choose everything you can say for sure.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.hint.0: Separate whether the words in each choice can be checked from the numbers in the table alone or need other information.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.hint.1: Put the numbers of the table you made directly into the choices to check.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.o.a: All 12 students picked one of the three places
y-m-03-08.s.s2.r.a: You connected the condition that the sum is 12 with the point that each person picked only one place.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.o.b: The zoo is more fun than the amusement park
y-m-03-08.s.s2.r.b: You turned 'more people picked it' into 'it is fun'. A table tells only the number of people who picked.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.o.c: More friends picked the zoo than picked the museum
y-m-03-08.s.s2.r.c: You compared two numbers in the table directly and said it.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.o.d: The friends who picked the museum have never been to the other places
y-m-03-08.s.s2.r.d: You made up an experience that is not in the table. A table tells only the places they want to go.
y-m-03-08.s.s2.explain: A table tells only 'how many students picked which place'. The sum is 12 students, so all picked one of the three places, and you can also say that the zoo has more than the museum. Fun or experience cannot be known from the table.

y-m-03-09.title: If one friend changes their mind, will the result change too?
y-m-03-09.topic: If one person's choice changes, will 'the most' change?
y-m-03-09.goal: Think through several cases to see that when the difference from the most is small, one person's choice can change the result, and when announcing results, say the size of the difference together.
y-m-03-09.material:
14 students in a group each picked one thing they want to do during break time.
[Table] Reading 6 students / Drawing 5 students / Puzzle 3 students (total 14 students)
Right now reading is the most by itself. But one friend says they will change their mind and pick something else. Only one friend changes their mind, and they want to pick something different from what they originally picked.
y-m-03-09.thinking.0: Think through all the possible cases
y-m-03-09.thinking.1: Find several cases that fit a condition
y-m-03-09.thinking.2: Choose a suitable expression when the difference is small
y-m-03-09.prereq.0: Counting data and reading a table
y-m-03-09.prereq.1: Adding 1 and subtracting 1 with numbers up to 15
y-m-03-09.s.s1.prompt: If one friend changes their mind, can the result 'reading is the most by itself' change?
y-m-03-09.s.s1.hint.0: Write all the pairs of what the person who might change their mind originally picked and what they newly pick.
y-m-03-09.s.s1.hint.1: For each pair, write one by one what the numbers for reading, drawing, and puzzle become.
y-m-03-09.s.s1.o.a: Reading has 6 students, which is plenty, so it can't change in any case
y-m-03-09.s.s1.r.a: You thought only that 6 students is many. You did not check what the numbers become if one is taken away or one is added to another.
y-m-03-09.s.s1.o.b: It may or may not change depending on who changes to where
y-m-03-09.s.s1.r.b: You looked at the point that the result can differ depending on who changes and what they newly pick. This judgment thinks in separate cases.
y-m-03-09.s.s1.o.c: If one person changes their mind, the result always changes in every case
y-m-03-09.s.s1.r.c: You decided that every case changes. If the change is made somewhere unrelated to reading, it can stay the same.
y-m-03-09.s.s1.o.d: We don't know who will change, so we can't think about what will happen
y-m-03-09.s.s1.r.d: You stopped thinking because there is something you don't know. You can split all the possible cases and think them through.
y-m-03-09.s.s1.explain: Reading (6 students) and drawing (5 students) are 1 student apart. If one is taken away from reading or one is added to drawing, the result changes, and if the change is made on the puzzle side, it can stay the same.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.prompt: Find 2 different cases where, after one friend changes their mind, 'reading is the most by itself' is no longer true. The numbers are reading=1, drawing=2, puzzle=3.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.hint.0: Decide on a pair (original, new) and write the new numbers for reading, drawing, and puzzle.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.hint.1: In the new numbers, compare one by one whether reading is more than both of the other two.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.var.f: Number of what they originally picked (1, 2, 3)
y-m-03-09.s.s2.var.t: Number of what they newly picked (1, 2, 3)
y-m-03-09.s.s2.fail.c1: The number must be one of 1, 2, 3.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.ok.c2: They picked something different from what they originally picked.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.fail.c2: They must pick something different from what they originally picked.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.ok.c3: After the change, reading is not the most by itself.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.fail.c3: Even after the change, reading is still the most by itself. Count the numbers again.
y-m-03-09.s.s2.explain: If 1 student is taken away from reading (reading to drawing: 5, 6, 3 / reading to puzzle: 5, 5, 4), or 1 is added to drawing (puzzle to drawing: 6, 6, 2), reading is not the most by itself. Drawing to puzzle gives 6, 4, 4, so reading is still the most by itself.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.prompt: When you announce the result of reading 6 students and drawing 5 students to your friends, what are suitable words?
y-m-03-09.s.s3.hint.0: Recall the cases you just found and say how firm the result is when the difference is 1 student.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.hint.1: For each choice, check whether it says both 'the most' and 'how much the difference is'.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.o.a: Reading is much more, so the result stays the same no matter who changes
y-m-03-09.s.s3.r.a: You saw the difference as big. As you just found, if one person changes, the result can change.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.o.b: Drawing is just as many as reading
y-m-03-09.s.s3.r.b: You treated a small difference as being the same. 6 students and 5 students are not the same number.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.o.c: The puzzle has only 3 students, so you can treat it as if it were none
y-m-03-09.s.s3.r.c: You treated a small number as none. Even 3 students can become different with one more change.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.o.d: Reading is the most, but it is 1 student apart from drawing
y-m-03-09.s.s3.r.d: You said the most and the size of the difference together. These words even thought about how firm the result is.
y-m-03-09.s.s3.explain: It is true that 6 students is the most, but it is only 1 student apart from 5 students, so if one person changes their mind it can change. If you also tell the size of the difference, you can pass on the result more accurately.
